content: Miscarriage, defined as the spontaneous loss of a pregnancy before 24 weeks of gestation, is a common occurrence, with approximately 25% of women experiencing a miscarriage at some point in their lives. Between 15% and 20% of pregnancies end in miscarriage. Progesterone plays a critical role in maintaining pregnancy, and supplementation with various forms of progestogens has been explored as a potential intervention to prevent miscarriage. This includes its use in women experiencing early pregnancy bleeding (threatened miscarriage) and in asymptomatic women with a history of three or more previous miscarriages (recurrent miscarriage). The objective of this study was to evaluate the relative effectiveness and safety of different progestogen treatments for both threatened and recurrent miscarriage. The study also aimed to rank the available treatments based on their effectiveness, safety, and side-effect profiles. A comprehensive search of databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, Ovid MEDLINE, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform, was conducted up to December 15, 2020. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) assessing the effectiveness or safety of progestogen treatments for miscarriage prevention were included. Cluster-randomized trials and RCTs published as abstracts (if sufficient data were available) were also eligible. However, quasi-randomized and non-randomized trials were excluded. Data from the included studies were independently assessed by at least two reviewers for inclusion and risk of bias. Pairwise meta-analyses and indirect comparisons were performed to evaluate the relative effects of the treatments. The primary outcome was live birth, while secondary outcomes included miscarriage (before 24 weeks), preterm birth (before 37 weeks), stillbirth, ectopic pregnancy, congenital abnormalities, and adverse drug events. The GRADE approach was used to assess the certainty of the evidence. The meta-analysis included seven randomized trials involving 5,682 women, all conducted in hospital settings. Across the 14 treatment arms in these trials, the following interventions were used: vaginal micronized progesterone (three arms, 21%), dydrogesterone (three arms, 21%), oral micronized progesterone (one arm, 7%), 17-α-hydroxyprogesterone (one arm, 7%), and placebo (six arms, 43%). For women with threatened miscarriage: Vaginal micronized progesterone, based on two trials involving 4,090 women, likely makes little or no difference to the live birth rate compared to placebo (risk ratio [RR] 1.03, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.00 to 1.07, high-certainty evidence). Dydrogesterone, based on one trial involving 406 women, also likely makes little or no difference to the live birth rate compared to placebo (RR 0.98, 95% CI 0.89 to 1.07, moderate-certainty evidence). There were no data available to assess the effectiveness of 17-α-hydroxyprogesterone or oral micronized progesterone for live birth outcomes in women with threatened miscarriage. Subgroup analysis for vaginal micronized progesterone showed that in women with no previous miscarriages and early pregnancy bleeding, there was likely little or no improvement in live birth rate compared to placebo (RR 0.99, 95% CI 0.95 to 1.04, high-certainty evidence). However, in women with one or more previous miscarriages and early pregnancy bleeding, vaginal micronized progesterone increased the live birth rate compared to placebo (RR 1.08, 95% CI 1.02 to 1.15, high-certainty evidence). For women with recurrent miscarriage: Vaginal micronized progesterone, based on one trial involving 826 women, likely makes little or no difference to the live birth rate compared to placebo (RR 1.04, 95% CI 0.95 to 1.15, high-certainty evidence). The evidence for dydrogesterone compared to placebo in women with recurrent miscarriage is of very low certainty, leaving the effects unclear. There were no data available to assess the effectiveness of 17-α-hydroxyprogesterone or oral micronized progesterone for live birth outcomes in women with recurrent miscarriage. Regarding additional outcomes: Progestogen treatments showed a wide range of effects on secondary outcomes, including miscarriage (before 24 weeks), preterm birth (before 37 weeks), stillbirth, and ectopic pregnancy, when compared to placebo for both threatened and recurrent miscarriage. Moderateand low-certainty evidence suggests that vaginal micronized progesterone likely does not increase the risk of congenital abnormalities or adverse drug events in women with threatened miscarriage (congenital abnormalities: RR 1.00, 95% CI 0.68 to 1.46; adverse drug events: RR 1.07, 95% CI 0.81 to 1.39) or recurrent miscarriage (congenital abnormalities: RR 0.75, 95% CI 0.31 to 1.85; adverse drug events: RR 1.46, 95% CI 0.93 to 2.29). However, data on other progestogens for these outcomes are limited and of very low certainty. In conclusion, the available evidence suggests that progestogens likely make little or no difference to the live birth rate for women with threatened or recurrent miscarriage. However, vaginal micronized progesterone may increase the live birth rate in women with a history of one or more previous miscarriages and early pregnancy bleeding, with no significant difference in adverse events. There remains uncertainty regarding the effectiveness and safety of other progestogen treatments for these conditions.
